content_voiceover: Now we add the brakes to the fibrinolysis pathway we just reviewed. Same core loop, thrombin converts fibrinogen to crosslinked fibrin, t-PA converts plasminogen to plasmin, and plasmin degrades the crosslinked fibrin, but now notice two new inhibitors attached at key points. PAI, plasminogen activator inhibitor, sits right on t-PA, neutralizing it before it can efficiently activate plasminogen. And alpha-2-antiplasmin, labeled here as alpha-2-AP, binds directly to free plasmin, shutting it down before it can cause widespread fibrin degradation. These two inhibitors are the fibrinolytic counterparts to antithrombin and protein C on the coagulation side, they keep fibrinolysis localized to the clot rather than letting it become a systemic process. Clinically, deficiency of either PAI or alpha-2-antiplasmin causes a bleeding tendency from unchecked fibrinolysis, while excess PAI-1 activity is associated with a prothrombotic state.
keypoints: PAI, plasminogen activator inhibitor, blocks t-PA
These inhibitors keep fibrinolysis localized rather than systemic
Deficiency of either causes a bleeding tendency from excess fibrinolysis
keypoint_voiceover: To summarize the brakes on fibrinolysis, PAI inhibits t-PA and alpha-2-antiplasmin inhibits plasmin, and losing either one tips the balance toward excessive, unchecked clot breakdown and bleeding.
